day-26-act-01.title: Random variables and probability distributions
day-26-act-01.prerequisites: Complete Day 25 (probability foundations); use the listed recovery link (Day 21) if blocked.
day-26-act-01.objective: Define a discrete random variable as a function from outcomes to numbers, validate a probability distribution table, and connect it to categorical distributions over tokens.
day-26-act-01.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-26-act-01.instructions: A random variable $X$ maps each outcome of the sample space to a number; its distribution lists $P(X=x)$ with $\sum_x P(X=x)=1$. For a fair die, $X$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,6\}$. Required work: compute $E[X]$ for the die, then validate the token-type distribution $p=[0.5,0.25,0.125,0.125]$ over values $\{0,1,2,3\}$.
day-26-act-01.exercise_prompt: (a) Compute $E[X]$ for a fair die and explain why a non-integer expectation does not contradict the outcomes. (b) For $p=[0.5,0.25,0.125,0.125]$ over $\{0,1,2,3\}$, verify $\sum p = 1$ and compute $P(X\ge 2)$. (c) Interpret $p$ as a categorical distribution over four token types: which value is the most likely token?
day-26-act-01.hint: $E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6$. $P(X\ge 2) = P(X=2)+P(X=3)$. The expectation is a probability-weighted long-run average, not a required outcome.
day-26-act-01.answer: (a) $E[X] = 21/6 = 3.5$: the expectation is a long-run average, not a die face. (b) $0.5+0.25+0.125+0.125=1$; $P(X\ge 2)=0.125+0.125=0.25$. (c) Token 0 is most likely at $p=0.5$ - a categorical distribution is exactly a probability table over discrete types, the shape language-model output layers produce.
day-26-act-01.mastery_criterion: You validate the normalization $\sum p = 1$, compute $P(X\ge2)=0.25$, and explain expectation as an average distinct from any single outcome.

day-26-act-02.title: Expectation, variance, and worked distribution tables
day-26-act-02.prerequisites: Complete the previous activity; use the listed recovery link if blocked.
day-26-act-02.objective: Compute $E[X]$, $E[X^2]$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$, and the standard deviation for discrete distributions without assistance.
day-26-act-02.instructions: Work each row of the distribution table before combining them. Required work: the four-type distribution below, a fair die, and a Bernoulli(0.25) variable. Record predicted values before computing and keep exact fractions where possible.
day-26-act-02.exercise_prompt: For $p=[0.5,0.25,0.125,0.125]$ over $\{0,1,2,3\}$ compute $E[X]$, $E[X^2]$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)$, $\sigma_X$. Then compute $\mathrm{Var}$ for a fair die ($E[X^2]=91/6$) and for $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.25)$.
day-26-act-02.mastery_criterion: All values match the reference fractions/decimals computed unaided; variance is reported in squared units and $\sigma$ in the original units.

day-26-act-03.title: Sampling, empirical distributions, and maximum likelihood
day-26-act-03.prerequisites: Complete the previous activity; use the listed recovery link if blocked.
day-26-act-03.objective: Build an empirical distribution with seeded sampling, compare it with the true distribution using the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and derive maximum-likelihood estimates for Bernoulli and unigram models, including the zero-count failure.
day-26-act-03.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-26-act-03.instructions: Run: python3 -c "import random, collections; random.seed(26); s=[random.randint(1,6) for _ in range(100)]; print(round(sum(s)/100,4), collections.Counter(s))". The sample mean of a die has standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n \approx 1.7078/10 \approx 0.1708$. For a coin with 36 heads in 60 flips the likelihood is $p^{36}(1-p)^{24}$, maximized at $\hat p = 36/60$. For unigrams, MLE sets $\hat p(w) = \mathrm{count}(w)/N$.
day-26-act-03.exercise_prompt: (a) Report the seeded sample mean and one empirical frequency that deviates from $1/6$. (b) Derive $\hat p$ for 36 heads in 60 flips by setting the log-likelihood derivative to zero. (c) In the corpus "the cat sat on the mat the cat ran" ($N=9$, six observed types), give the unigram MLE for 'the' and for 'dog'. What breaks if a model assigns 0 to a held-out token?
day-26-act-03.hint: $\frac{d}{dp}[36\ln p + 24\ln(1-p)] = 36/p - 24/(1-p) = 0$. 'dog' never appears: MLE gives 0, and as $q \to 0^+$, $-\ln q \to +\infty$ in the next day's loss ($\ln q \to -\infty$, and evaluating $-\ln$ at exactly $q=0$ is undefined, not merely $-\infty$); add-1 smoothing over a 7-type vocabulary assigns $\hat p(\text{dog}) = 1/16$.
day-26-act-03.answer: (a) Mean $3.47$ vs true $3.5$ (difference $0.03$, well under one standard error $0.1708$); face 3 appeared 9 times ($0.09$ vs $0.1667$, roughly two standard errors low - plausible fluctuation, not proof of bias). (b) $\hat p = 36/60 = 0.6$. (c) $\hat p(\text{the}) = 3/9 = 1/3$; $\hat p(\text{dog}) = 0$: MLE assigns unseen tokens zero probability, producing infinite loss on any held-out 'dog' - add-1 over a 7-type vocabulary gives $\hat p(\text{the}) = 4/16 = 0.25$, $\hat p(\text{dog}) = 1/16 = 0.0625$.
day-26-act-03.mastery_criterion: You report the seeded numbers honestly (mean $3.47$, the face-3 shortfall), derive $\hat p = 0.6$ from the log-likelihood, and explain the zero-count failure plus the add-1 fix.

day-26-act-04.title: Independent mastery check: estimation and sampling
day-26-act-04.prerequisites: Complete the previous activity; use the listed recovery link if blocked.
day-26-act-04.objective: Solve unseen estimation problems unaided and state the statistical assumptions behind each result.
day-26-act-04.instructions: No AI or references during this check; arithmetic only. Record predictions first, solve all four items, then review and pick a recovery link for misses. Preserve the first unaided attempt unchanged; afterwards, error review and any assisted recovery are a distinct phase, and a missed idea counts as remediated only after a fresh equivalent unaided check whose answer is not shown in advance. Second check (only after remediation; unaided, no hints): (a) For $p=[0.2,0.3,0.4,0.1]$ over $\{0,1,2,3\}$ compute $E[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. (b) Compute $P(\text{at least one 6 in 3 rolls})$. (c) 9 heads in 15 flips: give $\hat p$ and its approximate standard error. (d) In one sentence, explain why a finite-sample proportion need not equal the true $p$. This card gives no answer for the second check: grade it by the same standard as the mastery criterion (correct values, i.i.d. and finite-sample assumptions stated), and verify only after finishing, by a second method ($\mathrm{Var}=E[(X-E[X])^2]$ directly, or enumerating all $6^3$ outcomes). Remediate a missed (a) with day-26-act-01 (valid distribution tables) and day-26-act-02 (expectation, variance), (b) with day-25-act-02 (independence) and day-25-act-01 (counting), and (c)-(d) with day-26-act-03 (sampling, standard error, maximum likelihood).
day-26-act-04.exercise_prompt: (a) For $p=[0.1,0.2,0.4,0.3]$ over $\{0,1,2,3\}$ compute $E[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. (b) Compute $P(\text{at least one 6 in 4 rolls})$. (c) 14 heads in 20 flips: give $\hat p$ and one reason the true $p$ could still differ. (d) Explain in one sentence why a finite sample mean need not equal $E[X]$.
day-26-act-04.answer: (a) $E[X]=0.2+0.8+0.9=1.9$, $E[X^2]=0.2+1.6+2.7=4.5$, $\mathrm{Var}=4.5-3.61=0.89$. (b) $1-(5/6)^4 = 1-625/1296 \approx 0.5177$. (c) $\hat p=0.7$; with $n=20$ the standard error is $\sqrt{0.7\cdot0.3/20}\approx0.102$, so the true $p$ plausibly differs by several points. (d) A finite-sample mean is not guaranteed to equal $E[X]$ - it is a random variable that fluctuates around it and can equal it by chance - but under the stated i.i.d./finite-variance assumptions it converges to $E[X]$ as $n$ grows (law of large numbers).
day-26-act-04.mastery_criterion: Unaided values match $1.9$, $0.89$, $0.5177$, $0.7$; the i.i.d. and finite-sample assumptions are stated; misses route to a recovery link, and each missed idea is remediated only by a fresh equivalent unaided check.
